subtopic: How the parser changes your markup
prompt: The markup has no <tbody>. How many <tbody> elements are in the DOM after the browser parses it?

verify.program:
import { JSDOM } from 'jsdom' const dom = new JSDOM(`
a
`) const { document } = dom.window console.log(document.querySelectorAll('tbody').length)

options.why: The parser INSERTS a tbody around any rows that are not in a thead or tfoot. This is why a CSS rule like table > tr never matches anything.
This assumes the DOM matches what you typed. For tables the parser adds elements you did not write.
One tbody is added, not one per row.
Leaving out tbody is valid HTML. The parser quietly fills it in.

hint: The DOM is not always what you typed.

prompt: How many child elements does the <input> have?

verify.program:
import { JSDOM } from 'jsdom' const dom = new JSDOM(`

hi

`) const { document } = dom.window console.log(document.querySelector('input').children.length)

options.why: input is a void element: it can never contain anything. The <b> becomes its SIBLING, not its child, even though it is written after it.
This reads <input> as an opening tag that wraps what follows. A void element has no closing tag and no contents.
There is only one element after it in any case, and it is not inside.

options.text: An error, input needs a closing tag
options.why: It must NOT have one. Writing </input> is the mistake.

hint: Can an input ever contain anything?

verify.program:
import { JSDOM } from 'jsdom' const dom = new JSDOM(`

two
three

`) const { document } = dom.window console.log(document.querySelectorAll('p').length)

options.why:
A p cannot contain a div, so the parser CLOSES the p before the div, then the stray

at the end opens and closes an empty second one.
This assumes the nesting survives. The parser breaks the p apart instead, which is why text can jump out of its paragraph.
The p is not thrown away. It is split.
Only two p elements result: the one that was cut short and the empty one from the leftover closing tag.

hint: What must the parser do when a div appears inside a p?

prompt: Which attribute joins a <label> to its input?

verify.program:
import { JSDOM } from 'jsdom'
const dom = new JSDOM(`<label for="n">Name</label>
<input id="n">`)
const { document } = dom.window
console.log(document.querySelector('label').control.id)

options.why: The label’s for attribute must hold the input’s id. Then tapping the label focuses the field, which matters a lot on a phone.
The name attribute is what gets submitted with the form. It does not join a label to a field.
There is no attribute by that name here.
The pair really is joined, so the control is found and it has an id.

hint: for points at something. At what?

prompt: What is the alt attribute on an for?

options.text: Text read aloud or shown when the image cannot be seen
options.why: A screen reader reads it, and a browser shows it when the file fails to load. An image that carries meaning needs one.

options.text: The tooltip shown when you hover
options.why: That is the title attribute, and it is not a replacement, because it is not read by default.

options.text: The file name of the image
options.why: The file is named by src. alt describes what the image SHOWS.
Size comes from width and height, or from CSS.

hint: Alt is short for alternative. Alternative to what?

prompt: Why use <nav> and <main> instead of <div> everywhere?

options.text: They tell screen readers and search engines what each part is
options.why: A div says nothing. A nav lets a screen reader offer "skip to navigation", and search engines use the structure too.
They look the same as a div. Semantics and appearance are separate.
The speed is identical. The difference is meaning.

options.text: A div is no longer valid HTML
options.why: div is still fine and still needed where there is no meaning to express.

hint: Who else reads your HTML apart from the browser?

prompt: Two elements share id="x". What does getElementById return?

verify.program:
import { JSDOM } from 'jsdom' const dom = new JSDOM(`

first

second

`) const { document } = dom.window console.log(document.getElementById('x').textContent)

options.why: An id is supposed to be unique. When it is not, the browser does not complain, it just hands back the FIRST match and the second becomes unreachable this way.
The search stops at the first match in document order.

options.text: An error about the duplicate id
options.why: Nothing errors. That silence is what makes duplicate ids a hard bug to find.
getElementById returns one element or null. querySelectorAll is the one that returns a list.

hint: The browser will not warn you. What does it do instead?

prompt: A <button> inside a form has no type attribute. What type is it?

verify.program:
import { JSDOM } from 'jsdom'
const dom = new JSDOM(`<form>
  <button>Go</button>
</form>`)
const { document } = dom.window
console.log(document.querySelector('button').type)

options.why: A button with no type defaults to submit, so it reloads the page. This is why a plain button in a form seems to "refresh" unexpectedly. Write type="button" to stop it.
That is what most people expect and it is why this catches them out. You have to ask for it.
Reset is never a default. You must write it.
Every button has an effective type. Leaving the attribute out picks the default, it does not remove it.

hint: Why does a form seem to reload when you click a plain button?
